summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was also the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Reuters reported that the decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for the rights of adolescents, and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's trajectory runs against its own recent history. The country is cited comparatively as a regional pioneer on marriage equality and gender recognition, which makes the 2025 decrees and the record hate-crime year legible as a reversal rather than as a baseline condition.

The documented violence is concentrated on local trans and travesti communities and on activists and organisations, rather than on foreign visitors. The hate-crime total and the activist testimony describe a domestic pattern of exposure; no source in the inventory records an incident involving a trans tourist.

Practical first-person accounts of moving around Buenos Aires at all hours circulate in gay travel guides, but they offer general urban safety impressions rather than findings specific to trans visitors, and they predate or sit alongside the 2025 policy shifts without addressing them.
localsOnly:
Residents lose access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors under the February 2025 decree, which legal experts contest as unconstitutional. Families of transgender adolescents are the population directly affected.

A separate decree issued at the same time regulates the housing of transgender people in prisons, changing the custodial conditions that trans detainees face.

Registration of organisations working on these issues is recorded as negative in Outright International's current assessment, which affects the operating space of the groups named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins and their ability to deliver support services.

Anti-discrimination protection remains available to residents through national and provincial statutes, and the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio continues to document incidents, giving a reporting channel that does not depend on executive goodwill.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the February 2025 decrees survive constitutional challenge is unresolved in the available sources. Legal experts are recorded as calling them illegal and unconstitutional and as intending to petition the courts, but no ruling is sourced here.

The inventory does not state whether the core self-identification provisions of Law 26.743 for adults remain fully operative after the decrees, or only the provisions touching minors and prison housing. The distinction is not sourced and should be verified against the decree texts.

No source records how the current framework is applied to foreign nationals seeking document changes or entry on the basis of a changed gender marker, and no data is available on screening of trans travellers at Argentine border points.

The removal of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance in 2020 and its rejection by the Supreme Court in 2025 are sourced to one case; whether the aggravator is unavailable across all gender-motivated homicide prosecutions is not established here.
